# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical reading: Two-year follow-up of Varden and a Halden subset

This is the strongest document in the series. It does what the earlier critiques asked for: a registered follow-up, an independent hours measure, a two-year horizon, a pre-specified mechanism test, and explicit responses to the re-analysis and the meta-analysis. Its central finding is well supported: in discretionary work, a real but modest per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at 24 months.

The weak points are in interpretation:
- the meetings "confirmation" is partly an accounting identity and was tested on the same offices that generated the hypothesis;
- the control-group meeting audit is contamination that affects the decay estimate, and the report doesn't treat it as such;
- the log-hours measure needs defining;
- the Halden figures carry several unacknowledged selection layers.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets, 24m | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098 | ✓ +9.8% |
| Per hour, logs, 24m | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085 | ✓ +8.5% |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 | ✓ |
| Halden survivors | 0.968 / (34.9/40.3 = 0.866) = 1.118 | ✓ +11.8% |
| Counter arm cost | 12% more staff gives +9% cost per contact | ? Needs explaining |

On the counter cost: if 12% more staff simply restored contacts handled to baseline, cost per contact would rise about 12%, not 9%. The 9% implies throughput rises above baseline, perhaps because fewer calls are abandoned. That assumption should be stated.

## 1. The meetings "confirmation" is weaker than presented

**The mediator is partly inside the outcome.** Recurring meetings are counted in hours worked. Cutting 3.5 hours of meetings therefore lowers the denominator of output per hour directly, whether or not anyone works faster. Part of the "47% explained" is plausibly arithmetic, not a behavioural pathway. That's still a real finding, since time was reallocated away from low-output activity, but it should be described as such and not framed as a mechanism akin to fatigue.

A rough check suggests the meetings share might be even larger than 47%. It assumes meeting time is included in timesheet hours and uses baseline hours of about 37.9:

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Treated non-meeting hours, baseline | about 37.9 − 7.4 = 30.5 |
| Treated non-meeting hours, month 24 | about 33.4 − 3.9 = 29.5 |
| Change in non-meeting hours | about −3% |
| Change in output per FTE | −3.4% |
| Output per non-meeting hour | about 0% |

If this approximation holds, the meeting cut accounts for nearly all the per-hour gain. That would leave little room for the fatigue pathway (18%) and the unexplained share (35%). The authors should report output per non-meeting hour directly. The discrepancy with their mediation model needs explaining.

**This is not an out-of-sample test.** The protocol was filed at month 11, after the month-6 meeting data and the 9-month results were known. It tests the hypothesis on the **same seven treated offices** that generated it. Registration guards against analytic flexibility. It does not answer Varga & Holm's actual concern, which is replication in new units. "Survives a registered test" is accurate; "confirms" is too strong.

**"A larger sample of office-months" overstates the information.** There are still 14 clusters. Office-months within an office are not independent. The CIs (28–66%) should reflect cluster-level inference, and it's not stated that they do.

**Several other caveats apply:**
- The mediators are not independent: fewer meetings may reduce fatigue, so separately estimated shares aren't cleanly additive.
- Sequential ignorability is a strong assumption. The authors acknowledge this.
- Managers who cut meetings hardest may differ in ways that also raise output.

## 2. The control-office meeting audit is contamination

The report presents the month-15 audit as an interesting side observation. It is also contamination of the control arm, and it biases the 24-month DiD downward:

- Two of seven control offices raised output per hour by about 4.1% after month 15.
- Averaged across the control arm, that is roughly 1.2 points of improvement in the control group over the period.
- So part of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may reflect **controls improving**, not the treated offices' gain fading.

**Decay is also not statistically established on its own terms.** The 9-month CI (+6.9 to +18.4) and the 24-month CI (+4.6 to +15.2) overlap almost entirely. "Consistent with some fading" is fair. Section 5's "declined by about a quarter" overstates the precision.

**The summary mixes measures.** "Fell from 12.5% to 8.5%" compares timesheet hours at 9 months with log hours at 24 months. The like-for-like decline is from 12.5% to 9.8%.

**The audit offices are also informative on the policy question:**

| | Meeting hours cut | Per-hour gain linked to meetings |
|---|---|---|
| Treated offices | 3.5 h | about 4.0% (47% of 8.5%) |
| Audit offices (no hours cut) | 2.1 h | 4.1% |

Per hour of meetings removed, the audit offices gained at least as much as treated offices did. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and possibly regression to the mean. A simple improvement would be to compare them with the other five control offices over the same months. Still, it strengthens the case that much of the gain could be had by reorganising without cutting hours. The authors correctly say this can't be settled without a reorganise-only arm.

## 3. The log-hours measure needs defining

- **What do the logs capture?** The report says they record "time staff are working on cases." If so, they should **exclude meetings**. Then the 3.5-hour meeting cut wouldn't reduce log hours, and log hours should have fallen much less than timesheet hours. Instead they fell almost as much (−11% v −12%). Either the logs include time logged in during meetings, in which case they don't measure active case work, or the measure is something else. Its definition determines whether "per log-measured hour" is stricter or just different.
- **Was there a baseline?** The measure was "added" for the follow-up and is blank at 9 months. A DiD on log hours needs pre-period log data. If historical logs were retrieved, the report should say so. If not, the −11% isn't a DiD.

## 4. Halden subset: more selection than acknowledged

The authors honestly call the 11 continuing organisations an upper bound and "survivors twice over." There are more layers than that:

1. Organisations self-selected into the pilot.
2. Seven withdrew after the schedule had started. The original report misreported this, and this report, co-authored by Okafor, doesn't acknowledge it.
3. Only 23 submitted records.
4. Only 14 of those 23 responded at follow-up.
5. Three reverted, and the remaining 11 continued.

Further issues:
- **The hours baseline looks borrowed.** 40.3 is exactly the 27-organisation average from the re-analysis. Is it these 11 organisations' own baseline? Do all 11 have time tracking? The re-analysis found only 17 organisations with both records and time tracking.
- **Output rose relative to the pilot period.** The survivors' output at 24 months (96.8) is above the 95.1–95.4 from the pilot period. That may be learning or further selection, and the report can't distinguish them.
- **The work-type classification is imperfect.** A marketing agency reverting over client deadlines suggests "discretionary versus coverage-bound" is not a clean sector split. Client-facing deadlines create coverage-like constraints. This fits the meta-analysis's own limitation.
- **Including the reverters lowers the figure.** With output at 88–91 when they reverted, any whole-subset figure falls noticeably. Reporting one would be more informative than the survivor-only estimate.

## 5. The responses to earlier claims are mostly fair

**On the re-analysis.** The rebuttal is sound for discretionary work: randomised, record-based, independent hours, two years, and a gain whose CI excludes zero. But one of the re-analysis's recommended standards was analysis of all enrolled units. Varden's counter arm was terminated, so the 24-month claim is about **case-processing only**, and Section 5 should say so explicitly. The novelty rebuttal is fair as far as it goes: no collapse by month 10, though some possible fading.

**On the meta-analysis.** The supplementary table shows all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the suspicion in my earlier comments, and it substantially undercuts the meta-analysis's "no sign of decay." Note, though, that Varden is now the only controlled long-term study. The durability evidence is one employer and 14 offices.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Output per FTE is drifting.** It went from −2.1% to −3.4%, with a CI reaching −8.0%. With full pay maintained, cost per case has risen. Overtime may add to that. The report gives a cost estimate for the counter arm but not for case-processing, and the employer would need both.
- **Sick days and resignations** are still reported without CIs, and resignations still as raw levels, as at 9 months.
- **The counter arm** now has a proper control comparison for waiting times (7.3 v 4.0 minutes), which addresses an earlier gap. Its early termination is itself informative.

## Updated synthesis

| Question | Before this report | After this report |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8–12%, mostly short-term | About 8.5–10% at 24 months in one RCT; durable, possibly some fading |
| Novelty | Disputed; meta-analysis said "set aside" on weak evidence | No collapse; modest decline that is partly confounded by control contamination |
| Coverage-bound work | Output falls about 9–11% | Confirmed; county ended the arm; restoring service costs about +9% per contact |
| Mechanism | Unknown | Meetings are the largest identified contributor, partly by accounting; fatigue is minor |
| Is the hours cut necessary? | Not asked | Open; two uncontrolled control offices suggest reorganisation alone captures some of the gain |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | About −2% | About −3.4%, CI includes zero; trending toward a small loss |

## Bottom line

This report settles more than any earlier document. A gain in output per actual hour of roughly 8–10% persists for two years in randomised discretionary work. Coverage-bound work cannot absorb the cut without extra staff. Both "entirely an artifact" and "no decay" were wrong.

The report should:
1. describe the meetings result as substantially an accounting reallocation, and report output per non-meeting hour;
2. acknowledge that the confirmatory test reused the hypothesis-generating offices;
3. treat the control-office audit as contamination and adjust or bound the decay estimate for it;
4. define the log-hours measure and its baseline;
5. scope its rebuttal to case-processing;
6. report Halden figures including the reverters, and correct the record on Halden's attrition.

The key open question, which the authors rightly flag, is whether the gain comes from cutting hours or from the reorganisation that cutting hours forces. That calls for a three-arm trial: reduced hours, meeting and workflow reorganisation at full hours, and control. The evidence so far suggests reorganisation alone may capture a substantial share of the gain at no cost in output per worker.
